extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of political theology, church-state relations, and early-modern theological/political polemics
extracted.subtask_description: A textual/theological-political analysis arguing what powers the Pope may legitimately claim (spiritual, legislative, judicial, temporal) and whether those powers extend beyond his own civil dominion. The page analyzes scriptural texts and historical precedents to evaluate papal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of binding and loosing belongs to Supreme Pastors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power granted in Matth. 18.18 (and similar texts) belongs to all Supreme Pastors; such as are all Christian Civil Sovereigns in their own Dominions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual citation used to argue that the authority to 'bind' and 'loose' is not exclusive to St. Peter or the Pope but is inherent in the office of supreme pastors (i.e., sovereigns) within their territories; thus interpret binding/loosing in light of civil sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Sovereigns are supreme Pastors in their own dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian civil sovereigns, by virtue of their sovereignty and baptism, are supreme teachers/pastors within their territories and thereby have the right (and responsibility) to teach doctrine to their subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that baptism and sovereign office make princes responsible for the instruction of their subjects; permitting others to teach is at the prince's peril. This is used to limit external ecclesiastical claim to jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: St. Peter is not Monarch Universall of the Church
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that St. Peter was Monarch Universal of the Church (i.e., monarch of all Christians worldwide) is rejected—if Peter was given any supremacy, it did not extend to temporal sovereignty over all Christendom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to refute arguments that treat the papacy as an immediate temporal universal monarchy; distinguishes spiritual commission from worldly jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal jurisdiction requires civil sovereignty to be enforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical jurisdiction that carries force (laws, punishments) is effectively civil jurisdiction and can only be exercised where the Pope is also civil sovereign or where civil sovereigns have granted him that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between spiritual counsel and legally binding law; without civil enforcement the Pope's decrees remain counsel rather than law in another prince's dominions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Antichrist (two essential marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antichrist, in the proper signification, has two essential marks: (1) he denyeth Jesus to be Christ; (2) he professeth himself to be Christ (i.e., falsely pretends to be the Christ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definitional criterion is used to argue that the Pope cannot properly be called 'the Antichrist' since he neither denies Jesus nor claims to be Christ himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Antichrist identified by eschatological signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The special, single Antichrist (Antichrist definitely) is associated with specific signs/timing (e.g., the abominable destroyer standing in the holy place, unprecedented tribulation, darkening of sun and moon, falling stars, coming of Christ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal/eschatological markers must be present to identify the singular Antichrist; many popes have come and gone without these signs, so the special Antichrist is not yet come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal usurpation of worldly kingdom is 'for Christ' not 'as Christ'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Pope exercises worldly power and makes laws to Christian kings/nations, he usurpeth a kingdom 'as for Christ' rather than 'as Christ'—this is not equivalent to being Antichrist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes motive/character of papal temporal claims from the theological personation of Christ; usurpation of temporal rule does not equal the eschatological Antichrist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural texts must be properly interpreted for infallibility claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of papal infallibility rely on scriptural citations; such citations must be read in context and are often strained (e.g., Bellarmine's exegesis of Luke 22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page examines each text Bellarmine uses and argues alternative, non-infallibility interpretations (e.g., Luke 22 refers to strengthening faith, not granting jurisdictional infallibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Luke 22:31-32 interpreted as strengthening faith, not granting jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The text where Christ prays that Peter's faith not fail should be read as meaning Peter would preserve faith and 'confirm' brethren, not that Peter or his successors would define points of faith infallibly or hold temporal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes the narrative context (the supper, dispute about greatness and future kingdom) to show no grant of worldly authority or universal doctrinal infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew 16: 'Thou art Peter' signifies confession, not temporal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'rock' on which the Church is built is the confession that 'Jesus is Christ the Son of God' (Peter's confession), not a grant of universal temporal or juridical supremacy to Peter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that Matthew 16 supports the endurance of the confession against Hell's gates rather than establishing a monarchal office with universal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: John 21 'Feed my sheep' is a commission to teach, not make laws
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Feed my sheep' is a command to teach and is not a grant of legislative power to make laws for the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching authority does not equate to legislative (law-making) authority; making laws belongs to the lord of the family (civil sovereign) who appoints chaplains/teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exodus 28:30 (Urim and Thummim) supports civil sovereigns' evidential/truth function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Urim and Thummim as 'Evidence and Truth' given to the High Priest is read as an argument that evidence/truth (near-infallibility) was vested in the High Priest under a civil commonwealth; thus in Christian commonwealths similar functions belong to civil sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that scriptural precedents for 'evidence and truth' align with civil sovereign authority in an ordered commonwealth, not a universal papal infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: John 16:13 limited to 'all truth necessary to salvation'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spirit 'leading into all truth' should be mitigated to mean 'all truth necessary to salvation' and therefore does not justify broad papal infallibility or jurisdiction beyond salvific essentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the Pope could not err in such necessary matters, that would not entitle him to jurisdiction over another prince's dominions absent explicit command from Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason requirement: must show Christ commanded obedience to the Pope
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify submission to papal authority by reason, one must show when and where Christ commanded obedience to a Pope; otherwise the argument that papal fallibility would frustrate Christ's provision is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical/theological standard: claims about obligation require demonstration of a divine command directing obedience to that specific ecclesiastical office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereignty and supreme judicature in matters of manners are the same
rubrics_metrics.description: Civill Soveraignty and supreme judicature in controversies of manners coincide: makers of civil laws determine justice and injustice (righteousness) of actions within their realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that when the Pope claims supremacy in 'manners' (i.e., moral/legal conduct), he conflicts with the civil sovereign who legislates and determines right/wrong in that polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deut.17:12 concerns obedience to the civil sovereign (High Priest/King), not papal law over foreign realms
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage about hearkening to the priest/judge in Israel is contextualized to the High Priest as civil authority in Israel and therefore supports civil sovereignty's legislative role rather than a universal papal legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual/historical reading: Old Testament examples of religious authority were embedded in civil political structures, so they do not prove universal papal legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew 23:4 and 'binding' interpreted as civil legislative function
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'binding' attributed to scribes and Pharisees (binding heavy burdens) indicates making laws, which properly belongs to civil sovereigns (e.g., Moses/chairs under God), not to a universal ecclesiastical legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between admonishment/teaching and imposition of civil legal burdens; legislative acts have distinct character and source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts 15:28 is counsel, not law ('it hath seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apostolic Council's language of 'it hath seemed good' indicates advice/counsel aimed at the benefit of the recipients, not binding law imposed by legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes law's motive (benefit/instrument of prescriber) from counsel's motive (benefit of recipient); use of conditional/persuasive language supports the counsel reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between law and counsel based on reason/motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is justified by the design and benefit of him who prescribes it; counsel is justified by the design and benefit of him to whom it is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative test is offered to classify apostolic/epistolary directives: if the aim is the recipient's salvation, treat as counsel; if the aim is the prescriber's interest/authority, treat as law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romans 13 implies obedience to civil higher powers, not dual masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Romans 13's command to be subject to higher powers is best read as referring to secular rulers; to interpret it as requiring obedience to both one's prince and the Pope would be impossible ('serve two masters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermeneutic principle: scripture must be interpreted to avoid logical or moral contradictions like serving two masters; thus civil obedience is primary in polity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication is not equivalent to civil punishment absent civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication, lacking civil enforcement, is essentially a denouncing of punishment to be inflicted by Christ at judgment and not a civil sanction like death or imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates spiritual censures (which may have strong social effects) from legally enforced civil punishments; thus ecclesiastical penalties do not equate to legislative jurisdiction without civil backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'rod' in 1 Cor. 4:21 as ecclesiastical sanction, not civil coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'rod' in Paul's question ('shall I come to you with a rod...') is taken to mean excommunication or spiritual censure, not the coercive instruments of civil magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that apostolic authority concerns reputation and spiritual discipline, not law-enforcement powers of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary precepts to church officers are often counsel, not law (e.g., 1 Tim. 3:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions like 'A Bishop must be the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober' are wise precepts for church governance and training (Timothy's charge) rather than universal legislative commands binding as civil law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context (teacher-disciple relationship, not civil subject-subject) is decisive: precepts to disciples/scholars should not be elevated to juridical universal law without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek lexical distinctions matter in judging 'obedience' and 'commands'
rubrics_metrics.description: Words translated as 'obey' or 'command' (e.g., upakouei, paraggelias) can mean 'hearken to' or 'put into practice' and therefore do not necessarily imply civil-legal obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philological criterion: examine original language to determine whether apostolic directives are juridical commands or moral/catechetical exhortations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrews 13:17's 'obey your leaders' refers to following counsel for salvation, not legal compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obey your leaders... for they watch for your souls' grounds obedience in the benefit to the believer (salvation) rather than in a prescriptive legal power to coerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that pastoral leadership's authority is persuasive and prudential; if it were legal in nature, then every pastor would have legislative powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction properly defined as power to hear and determine causes; requires law-making and coercive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction is the power of hearing and determining causes between man and man and belongs only to those who can prescribe rules of right and wrong and compel obedience (i.e., civil sovereigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative legal-political test: if an authority lacks the power to make laws and enforce them with the sword, it does not possess full jurisdiction in the civil sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops' jurisdiction derives from civil sovereigns in each commonwealth (Numbers 11 analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old Testament precedent (Moses choosing elders) shows authority delegated under a sovereign; likewise, bishops in a Christian commonwealth derive jurisdiction from the civil sovereign of that place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical-analogical criterion: where civil structures provided religious authority in Israel, similar derivation is expected in Christian polities; thus episcopal jurisdiction is mediated by local sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy-nature argument: derivation of authority favors civil monarchs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because monarchy places authority in one man and derives other authority from him, reading Church government as monarchic actually supports the authority of Christian monarchs over ecclesiastical offices within their realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political-theoretical criterion: if church government is monarchic in practice, then civil monarchs are the proper sources of derivative jurisdiction in their territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality of diocesan jurisdictions implies human, not divine, origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation in the size and scope of bishops' jurisdictions (some over one town, some over many provinces) indicates jurisdictional arrangements are determined by human/princely institutions rather than immediate divine ordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical/political criterion: observable inequalities in jurisdictions support the conclusion that jurisdiction is conferred by princes or civil polity, not uniformly by God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pope cannot remove bishops' jurisdiction in other sovereigns' dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: If bishops' jurisdiction in a territory derives from that territory's sovereign, the Pope lacks authority to deprive or alter those jurisdictions in other princes' dominions except where sovereign power has been granted to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits papal claims to interfere with local ecclesiastical structures unless the civil sovereign has conceded that power; underscores dependency of ecclesiastical jurisdiction on civil grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal temporal power limited to own territory; no direct temporal jurisdiction elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions: the Pope is not lord of all the world nor of all the Christian world; he has no direct temporal jurisdiction outside his own territory, and any temporal power 'indirectly' must be by indirect/conferred means, which is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes temporal-political conclusion: papal temporal authority is limited; claims of universal temporal lordship are denied unless obtained by indirect (political) means.
